cards.body: Growth is a learning sport. The team that learns fastest wins. Today you'll learn how to design, run, and learn from experiments at high tempo — without sacrificing rigour or creating chaos.

cards.headline: The Anatomy of a Good Experiment
cards.body: Every experiment needs six components: 1) Hypothesis — "We believe [change] will cause [outcome] because [reason]." 2) Success metric — the one number that determines pass/fail. 3) Control vs. variant — what's the baseline? What are we testing? 4) Minimum sample size — how many users needed for statistical significance? 5) Duration — how long will we run it? 6) Decision criteria — if success metric improves by X%, we ship. Pre-committing to decision criteria prevents "we need more data" paralysis and HiPPO-driven reversals after the results come in.

cards.headline: The High-Tempo Testing Framework
cards.body: Sean Ellis's high-tempo testing principle: run experiments in parallel, learn from all of them, compound the winners. The bottleneck isn't ideas — it's implementation speed. Tactics for speed: 1) Modular tests — design experiments that can be launched in < 2 days of engineering time. 2) No-code tests — use tools like Optimizely, VWO, or even manual split routing for initial validation before building. 3) Test copy and positioning first — words are the cheapest experiments. 4) Feature flags — ship experiments to 10% of users without deploying twice. Speed × volume = learning rate.

cards.headline: Learning From Failures (The Most Important Part)
cards.body: Most experiments fail. That's not a problem — it's the process. A failed experiment still teaches you something if you've specified your hypothesis correctly. Failed experiment insights compound into better hypotheses over time. The mistake teams make: treating a failed experiment as wasted effort rather than a data point. Protocol for failed experiments: 1) Document why you expected it to work. 2) Document the actual result. 3) Generate 2-3 hypotheses about why it didn't work. 4) These become the next experiments. A well-documented failure is worth more than an undocumented win.

cards.headline: Try It: Design Your First Experiment
cards.body: Using your ICE-prioritised backlog from Lesson 15, take your top-scored idea and fill in: Hypothesis: "We believe [specific change] will [improve X metric] because [reason based on evidence]." Success metric: _______ Baseline (current value): _______ Target (what counts as a win): _______ Sample size needed: _______ Duration: _______ Decision date: _______ If you can't fill in all six, your experiment isn't ready to run. The discipline of pre-specifying everything is what separates learning from guessing.

quiz.question: Why should decision criteria for an experiment be pre-committed before results come in?
options: To prevent "we need more data" paralysis and biased post-hoc interpretation of results
Because results are only valid if criteria were set in advance for legal reasons
To make experiments run faster by skipping analysis
Because pre-commitment improves statistical accuracy
quiz.explanation: Pre-committing decision criteria prevents the common trap of re-interpreting results to fit what people hoped for ("HiPPO reversals") or endlessly extending experiments when results are inconvenient.

quiz.question: What is the fastest type of experiment to run for initial growth validation?
options: Copy and positioning tests — changing words costs nothing and can be done immediately
Full product feature builds tested on 100% of users
Paid acquisition experiments with large budgets
Complete UX redesigns validated with user research
quiz.explanation: Words are the cheapest experiments. Testing different headlines, value propositions, or email subjects requires zero engineering time and can validate positioning before investing in product or paid channels.

quiz.question: A failed experiment provides no useful information for future growth strategy.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A well-documented failed experiment is highly valuable — it confirms what doesn't work, generates hypotheses about why, and compounds into better future experiments. Treating failures as waste rather than data points is what kills growth team effectiveness.

lessons.title: Analysing Results & Compounding Wins
lessons.subtitle: The difference between good and great growth teams is not running more experiments — it's extracting more value from each one.

cards.headline: Amazon's "Customers who bought this also bought..." feature — one insight from a single data analysis — generates an estimated 35% of all Amazon revenue.
cards.body: Running experiments is only half the job. Extracting, applying, and compounding the learnings is where the real growth lives. Today you'll learn how to analyse results correctly, avoid common statistical traps, and build a learning flywheel that compounds over time.

cards.headline: Statistical Significance vs. Practical Significance
cards.body: A result can be statistically significant (not due to chance) but practically insignificant (too small to matter). Common mistakes: 1) Declaring victory too early — looking at results before reaching sample size. 2) Ignoring effect size — a 0.1% improvement that's "statistically significant" at n=1,000,000 is still a 0.1% improvement. 3) Celebrating p < 0.05 without asking "is this large enough to act on?" Rule of thumb: only act on results where the uplift exceeds your minimum meaningful threshold (typically 5-10% improvement on your success metric).

cards.headline: The Learning Extraction Framework
cards.body: After every experiment (win or loss), document: 1) What we tested (specific change). 2) What we measured (metric, baseline, result). 3) What we learned (the underlying insight, not just the result). 4) What we'll do next (the experiments this insight generates). Example: Tested: Adding social proof to pricing page. Result: +12% conversion. Learned: Customers at the decision stage are primarily motivated by peer validation, not feature lists. Next: Test testimonials segmented by customer type. The insight is more valuable than the 12% win — it shapes the next 10 experiments.

cards.headline: Building a Growth Wiki
cards.body: Institutional knowledge is a growth moat. Every insight, every failure, every surprising result should live in a shared "Growth Wiki" that new team members can read. Structure: Hypothesis log (what we tested, what we believed, what happened). Insight library (underlying learnings, with evidence). Channel performance database (cost/acquisition, conversion rate, volume by channel over time). Most companies lose their growth knowledge when team members leave or memory fades. A Growth Wiki compounds — each insight makes the next experiment smarter. Build it from day one.

cards.headline: Try It: Create Your First Growth Wiki Entry
cards.body: Think of the last marketing or product change you made. Document it in this format: What we changed: _______ Why we thought it would work: _______ Result (metric change): _______ Underlying insight: _______ Next experiment it suggests: _______ Paste this into a shared doc, Notion page, or spreadsheet. This is your Growth Wiki — one entry. Add one entry after every experiment from now on. In 6 months, this document will be one of your most valuable assets.

quiz.question: What is the difference between statistical significance and practical significance in experiments?
options: Statistical significance means the result is not due to chance; practical significance means the improvement is large enough to act on
Statistical significance is for scientists; practical significance is for businesses
They mean the same thing in the context of growth experiments
Statistical significance requires more data than practical significance
quiz.explanation: A result can be statistically significant (reliably not random) but practically meaningless (e.g., a 0.1% improvement). Growth decisions should require both: the result is not due to chance AND the effect is large enough to justify rollout.

quiz.question: What makes a "Growth Wiki" a competitive moat?
options: It compounds institutional knowledge so every new experiment is informed by all previous learnings
It is a secret database that competitors cannot access
It automatically runs experiments without human involvement
It stores customer data that other companies don't have
quiz.explanation: A Growth Wiki compounds institutional knowledge — each documented insight makes future experiments smarter, reducing wasted tests and accelerating discovery. Teams without one lose their learnings when people leave or memory fades.

quiz.question: You should declare a test a winner as soon as results look positive, before reaching the pre-committed sample size.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Declaring victory early (before reaching minimum sample size) produces false positives. Early results are noisy and often reverse as more data comes in. Always run to the pre-committed sample size and decision date.

lessons.title: Building a Scalable Acquisition Machine
lessons.subtitle: Tie it all together. Build the end-to-end acquisition system that runs, learns, and compounds without needing you in the room.

cards.headline: At peak growth, Dropbox was acquiring a new user every second — on autopilot — through a system they built and documented over 3 years.
cards.body: You've learned positioning, channels, referral mechanics, lifecycle emails, growth teams, and experiments. Today you'll learn how to assemble everything into a single, documented, scalable acquisition machine that doesn't depend on any one person.

cards.headline: The Acquisition Machine Blueprint
cards.body: A scalable acquisition machine has four layers: 1) Positioning layer — clear category, value proposition, and segment messaging. Updated quarterly. 2) Discovery layer — primary channel(s) that reliably drive new eyeballs (SEO, paid, partnerships, viral). 3) Conversion layer — landing pages, onboarding, and activation flows that convert discovery into activated users. 4) Retention & expansion layer — email sequences, habit loops, and referral mechanics that compound LTV. Each layer feeds the next. A breakdown in any layer throttles the whole machine. Audit each layer quarterly.

cards.headline: The Playbook: Documenting for Scale
cards.body: A machine that lives in someone's head isn't a machine — it's a dependency. Document: 1) Channel playbooks — step-by-step how each channel is managed, measured, and optimised. 2) Experiment templates — standard hypothesis, metric, and decision criteria formats. 3) Onboarding scripts — what a new team member needs to know to contribute from Day 1. 4) The Growth Wiki (from Lesson 20). With this documentation, your acquisition machine can be operated, improved, and scaled by others. This is the difference between a business and a job.

cards.headline: The Quarterly Growth Review
cards.body: Scaling requires regular recalibration. Every quarter: 1) Review your North Star Metric — are you on track? 2) Audit your channel stack — is your primary channel still the best? Are new channels ready to promote? 3) Review CAC and LTV trends — is unit economics improving or degrading? 4) Update your ICE backlog — new insights mean new experiments. 5) Review competitor positioning — has anything changed that requires a positioning update? The companies that stay at the top don't run growth once and coast. They treat growth as a continuous, disciplined system.

cards.headline: Try It: Your 30-Day Acquisition Sprint
cards.body: Design your acquisition sprint for the next 30 days: Week 1: Finalise your positioning statement using the canvas from Module 1. Write or update your landing page. Week 2: Run a Bullseye exercise. Identify your primary channel. Launch one small experiment. Week 3: Set up your welcome email sequence (5 emails). Identify your Aha Moment. Remove one friction point from activation. Week 4: Run your first weekly growth meeting. ICE-score your next 10 ideas. Launch one experiment. By Day 30, you won't have a perfect machine — but you'll have a running one. That's what matters.

quiz.question: What are the four layers of a scalable acquisition machine?
options: Positioning, Discovery, Conversion, and Retention & Expansion
Awareness, Consideration, Purchase, and Loyalty
Brand, Content, Paid, and Referral
Product, Marketing, Sales, and Customer Success
quiz.explanation: The four layers are: Positioning (clear category and value prop), Discovery (channels driving new eyeballs), Conversion (turning discovery into activated users), and Retention & Expansion (compounding LTV through email, habits, and referrals). Each feeds the next.

quiz.question: What makes an acquisition machine truly "scalable"?
options: It is documented in playbooks so it can be operated and improved by others without key-person dependency
It runs on fully automated paid advertising with no human input
It works across all 19 traction channels simultaneously
It generates more than £1M in annual revenue
quiz.explanation: Scalability comes from documentation — channel playbooks, experiment templates, and onboarding scripts that allow anyone to operate and improve the system. An acquisition approach that lives in one person's head is a dependency, not a machine.

quiz.question: Once you've built a working acquisition system, you can stop experimenting and focus on execution.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Growth requires continuous recalibration — quarterly reviews of channels, unit economics, competitor positioning, and new experiment backlogs. Markets change, channels saturate, and customer needs evolve. The top companies treat growth as a permanent, disciplined system.
